realTx.fee: , including a <fee/> box that is the miner's fee

intro.p1: When you open your banking app, you see one number: your balance. The bank keeps a spreadsheet where each row is an account, and moving money means subtracting from one row and adding to another.
intro.p2: Ergo doesn't work like that. There are no “accounts” on Ergo at all. Instead, money lives inside boxes.

what.title: What is a box?
what.p1: Imagine each box as a small glass case:
what.inside: Inside is some amount of ERG (and possibly other tokens too).
what.lock: On the outside is a lock. The lock is a piece of logic (a script) that says who may open the box.
what.visible: Anyone can see what's inside, but only someone who satisfies the lock can take it.
what.p2: The “balance” your wallet shows you is really just the total value of all the boxes your keys can open. The wallet adds them up for your convenience.

spend.title: Spending = breaking old boxes, sealing new ones
spend.p1: Boxes have one important property: they can't be partially opened. You can't take 3 ERG out of a 7 ERG box and leave the other 4 ERG inside. Instead, a transaction:
spend.inputs: Opens (and destroys) one or more old boxes — the inputs.
spend.outputs: Creates new boxes with new locks — the outputs.
spend.p2: The total going in must equal the total coming out. Whatever is left over is returned to you in a new box, called change — just like paying for a $3 coffee with a $20 bill and getting the difference back.
spend.p3: Look closely: the transaction fee is a box too! On Ergo, the fee is sent to a special box that only a miner can open. The block's miner collects every fee box in that block into a single reward box of their own — and that reward box stays locked for 720 blocks (about a day).

utxo.title: UTXO and eUTXO
utxo.p1: Boxes that haven't been spent yet are called UTXOs (Unspent Transaction Outputs). Bitcoin uses this model too. The set of all UTXOs is the current “state” of the blockchain: who owns what.
utxo.p2: Ergo extends it, hence the name eUTXO (extended UTXO): an Ergo box can hold tokens, can store arbitrary data in “compartments” called registers, and its lock can be an entire smart contract rather than just a signature.

good.title: Why is this design good?
good.predictable: Predictable: before you send, you know exactly which boxes are spent and which are created. No surprises.
good.parallel: Parallel: transactions that touch different boxes don't affect each other.
good.safe: Safe: a box can be spent exactly once. Spending it twice (a double-spend) is rejected by the network immediately.
good.p1: Developer David Przybilla sums this view up neatly in <article>Learning Ergo 101: eUTXO explained for human beings</article>: to an app builder, Ergo is just a dataset of boxes, the only operation is a transaction, and you simply describe “what the world should look like afterwards” — the script in each box decides whether that is allowed.

deeper.title: Want to go deeper?
deeper.text: The technical article <box>Boxes & registers</box> explains every field from R0 to R9, and <ergotree>ErgoTree & ErgoScript</ergotree> covers how the “locks” are written.

reading.title: Further reading
reading.meta: — David Przybilla, December 2021. A programmer's view of the same idea: the blockchain as a dataset of boxes, the transaction as the only operation, and scripts as simple true/false validators — a great read right after this page.
